name: Session 0: Old Friends, One Last Road

pages.name: Session 0 Overview: Old Friends, One Last Road
pages.html:
Session 0 is part campaign contract, part technical rehearsal, part collaborative character creation, and part playable prologue. Do not rush through the creative half: the purpose is to make Ispin Greenshield a person the players remember before the campaign asks them to mourn him.

BlockTargetPurpose
Welcome & campaign pitch15–20 minEstablish tone, premise, and expectations.
Table rules, safety, problem solving25–35 minAgree how the table works before play begins.
Foundry / Discord / Meet onboarding30–40 minMake every player technically ready.
Character foundations30–40 minTurn sheets into people with useful motives.
Ispin & party shared-history workshop45–60 minCreate bonds, inside jokes, and 2–3 past adventures.
Break10 minReset before roleplay.
Playable prelude: The Last Road to Vogler90–120 minMeet on the road, arrive together, explore Vogler, and sleep before the funeral.

Minimum Outcome

  • Every player can operate their Foundry sheet.
  • Every character has a reason to attend Ispin's funeral.
  • Every character has at least two PC connections.
  • The group creates at least two prior adventures with Ispin; three is ideal.
  • The party reaches Vogler on 17 Darkember, explores it, and spends the night at the Brass Crab.

Session 1 should begin with the funeral. Session 0 should make the players care who is being buried.

pages.name: Campaign Pitch and Player Promise
pages.html:
The campaign begins small: old friends walking to a funeral in a fishing village. It then expands into war, a long road south, the politics of High Sorcery, the Forest of Wayreth, and the Night of the Eye.

Player-Facing Pitch

You are level 1 adventurers who already know one another and who each knew Ispin Greenshield. You have completed a few modest adventures together. You are traveling to Vogler because Ispin has died. You do not begin as generals, chosen saviors, or famous heroes. You begin as people coming to say goodbye.

What This Campaign Rewards

  • Engagement: follow leads, make choices, and care about the consequences.
  • Character commitment: personality matters even when it complicates the easy solution.
  • Team play: protagonists can disagree without trying to destroy the party.
  • Curiosity: the world contains information worth asking for.
  • Time awareness: after Vogler, the calendar matters. Delays are choices, not arbitrary punishment.

Expected Opening Arc

Vogler → invasion → choice of three roads → 34–35 day journey south → border of Wayreth → Tower and Test → Night of the Eye.

Tone

Classic Dragonlance adventure with grounded relationships, war pressure, humor between characters, dangerous magic, travel, politics, and moments of genuine loss. Humor is welcome; treating every emotional scene as a joke is not.

pages.name: Table Rules: Respect, Focus, and Shared Play
pages.html:
These are the standing table rules for the campaign. Present them plainly, invite questions, and then treat them as normal expectations rather than a weapon to be quoted at players.

  1. Respect other players. Treat everyone with respect in and out of character. Personal attacks, derogatory language, and belittling are not acceptable.
  2. Listen to others. When someone has the floor, give them space to finish. Avoid interrupting or talking over other players.
  3. Stay focused. Keep phones and unrelated devices from becoming a distraction. Brief real-life interruptions happen; prolonged disengagement should not become routine.
  4. Be prepared. Arrive with your character sheet, access to Foundry, and any materials you personally use. Know your core features well enough to take a turn without rebuilding your character at the table.
  5. Follow the DM's lead. The DM adjudicates the world, NPCs, and uncertain rules. Questions and respectful rules corrections are welcome; repeated argument after a ruling is not.
  6. Stay in character where practical. Speak and act from your character's point of view when roleplaying, while still communicating clearly as players when consent, rules, or safety needs to be discussed.
  7. Take turns. During combat and busy social scenes, share space so everyone has opportunities to act and speak.
  8. Keep the game moving. Make decisions in reasonable time, know what your abilities do, and avoid side conversations that stall the table.
  9. Have fun. D&D is collaborative entertainment. The goal is for the whole table to enjoy the campaign, not for one character to "win" against everyone else.

Shared Spotlight

Players who naturally speak often should create openings for quieter players. Quieter players will be offered opportunities, but are not required to perform on command. The DM may deliberately cut between characters to keep scenes balanced.

pages.name: Problem Solving, Disagreements, and Escalation
pages.html:
Problems are easiest to resolve when they are raised early and privately rather than allowed to become part of the fiction.

  1. Raise concerns privately. If you have an issue during or after play, speak to the DM privately by message or separate conversation.
  2. Respect players and characters. Do not use "I was in character" as cover for personal attacks, humiliation, or belittling another player.
  3. Rules disputes. Check the official D&D rules when useful. If the answer remains unclear or would take too long to research, the DM makes the ruling for that session. The rule can be reviewed afterward.
  4. Breaks. If you need to step away, let the DM and group know in advance when possible. If something is urgent, simply step away and message when able.
  5. Unresolved conflict. If an issue cannot be handled respectfully while play continues, the DM may pause or end the session so the problem can be addressed properly.
  6. Streaming. The game is being streamed. Avoid behavior or language that would be inappropriate or offensive for the agreed audience and platform.

At-the-Table Rules Procedure

Question → quick check if needed → DM ruling → continue play → research afterward. A wrong ruling can be corrected going forward. Replaying an entire scene because of a small rules mistake is normally less useful than keeping the campaign moving.

Character Conflict

Characters may argue, distrust one another, compete, and hold different beliefs. Meaningful PvP—including attacks, theft, deliberate destruction of another PC's possessions, or hostile magic that removes another PC's agency—requires the affected player's consent.

pages.name: Campaign House Rules
pages.html:
These house rules replace the standard rule where they conflict with it. Make sure every player understands them before the prelude begins.

#RuleAt the Table
1Powerful CriticalsCritical hits deal maximum possible damage rather than rolling the critical damage dice.
2Critical FailuresOn an attack-roll natural 1, the DM may introduce an immediate mishap: losing/dropping the weapon, striking yourself, or endangering/damaging an ally, as fiction and positioning make appropriate.
3Potions in CombatAdministering a potion to an ally costs 1 Action. Drinking one yourself costs 1 Bonus Action.
4Quick Skill ChecksIn most circumstances a basic check such as Insight or Perception can be attempted during combat without consuming an action. Multitasking may impose disadvantage, a reduced result, or another situational penalty at the DM's discretion.
5Potion ToxicityIf you consume more than one potion within an hour, roll on the Potion Toxicity table.
6Maximum Potion HealingHealing potions restore their maximum listed healing; do not roll their healing dice.
7Stacking InspirationInspiration can stack. Inspiration is especially likely when a player commits to personality, ideals, bonds, or flaws despite a meaningful detrimental consequence, or contributes strongly to roleplay.
8Blind Death SavesDeath saves are rolled blind so the table does not know whether a fallen character is succeeding or failing.

House-Rule Intent

These rules make combat swingier, potions more useful, and character commitment more rewarding. Players should understand that critical failures can create consequences beyond a simple miss, while blind death saves deliberately remove metagame certainty.

pages.name: Safety, Consent, and Campaign Content
pages.html:
The campaign includes war, grief, dangerous magic, and loss. Safety tools are not a sign that the game has gone wrong; they are part of keeping intense fiction enjoyable.

Likely Campaign Content

  • Funerals, grief, and death.
  • War, occupation, military violence, refugees, and civilian danger.
  • Undead, monsters, and occasional magical body horror.
  • Imprisonment, coercion, curses, and mind-affecting magic.
  • Religious and political conflict within the setting.

Lines

Content that does not appear in the game. Establish these privately or together.

Veils

Content that may exist but is not described in detail or is handled off-screen.

Pause / Rewind

Any player can ask to pause, skip, rewind, or redirect a scene. They do not need to publicly justify the request.

Open Door

A player can step away from the table when necessary. The DM will catch them up afterward.

Private Contact

Players may message the DM during a scene instead of announcing a concern to the group.

pages.name: Attendance, Communication, and Streaming
pages.html:
Resolve campaign logistics during Session 0 so they do not become recurring uncertainty.

Attendance

  • Confirm the normal game day and expected session duration.
  • Ask for as much notice as practical when a player cannot attend.
  • Establish whether absent characters fade into the background, are run by another player with permission, or remain unavailable.
  • Establish the minimum number of players required for the session to go ahead.

Discord

Use Discord as the campaign headquarters. Recommended channels: Announcements, Scheduling, General, Character Discussion, Rules Questions, Session Recaps, and Useful Links.

Google Meet / Voice

Check microphone quality, headphones, muting, and noise suppression during Session 0 rather than during the funeral.

Streaming

Remind the table before the playable prelude that the session is streamed. Confirm player consent to the chosen display names, cameras if any, and the handling of private messages. Private player-to-DM messages remain private unless the player chooses to make them part of the broadcast.

pages.name: Foundry VTT: Technical Onboarding
pages.html:
Every player should physically perform the common Foundry actions during Session 0. Watching the DM demonstrate them is not enough.

Connection Checklist

  1. Open the Foundry campaign link.
  2. Log into the assigned player account.
  3. Confirm the correct Actor is visible.
  4. Open the character sheet.
  5. Confirm token ownership and control.
  6. Confirm journal and compendium access intended for players.

Character Sheet Tour

Show: abilities, saving throws, skills, AC, HP, Hit Dice, death saves, Actions, Inventory, Features, Spells, Effects, Biography, and currency.

Campaign Tools

Show the Journals tab, player handouts, calendar, map notes, and the spell/item compendia. Explain that shared information appears in journals rather than needing to be copied into chat.

Troubleshooting Order

  1. Refresh Foundry.
  2. Check browser permissions and extensions.
  3. Clear the site cache only if necessary.
  4. Try a supported Chromium browser if the current browser remains problematic.
  5. Message the DM with the exact error instead of repeatedly reconnecting without explanation.

pages.name: Foundry VTT: Training Drill
pages.html:
Use a simple training scene before character history. Five minutes spent actually rolling now can save half an hour later.

Movement

Each player moves their token, uses the ruler, opens a door if available, and pings a location.

Checks

Each player rolls one ability check, one skill check, and one saving throw.

Combat Drill

  1. Target a harmless training dummy.
  2. Roll initiative.
  3. Take one movement and one action.
  4. Make one attack and roll damage.
  5. End the turn.

Spellcasting Drill

Every spellcaster casts a cantrip and a leveled spell, places one template if relevant, identifies concentration, and sees where spell-slot expenditure is recorded.

Healing and Conditions

Damage one volunteer token, heal it, apply Prone, remove Prone, and show where Active Effects appear.

Blind Death-Save Demonstration

Show how the campaign handles a blind death save so players understand they will see the roll occur without receiving the result.

Resting

Show Short Rest and Long Rest controls without leaving the final character state altered.

pages.name: Character Foundations: Who Were You Before This?
pages.html:
Do not ask for a five-page biography. Ask questions that generate playable decisions.

Thirty-Second Introduction

Each player gives: Name, species, class, home, what strangers notice first, and one common misconception about them.

Six Foundation Questions

  1. Before adventuring, what did you think your life would become?
  2. Why did you begin adventuring?
  3. What are you good at that has nothing to do with combat?
  4. What are you currently trying to prove?
  5. What do you fear people will eventually discover about you?
  6. What would make you abandon a safe life and travel across Ansalon?

Krynn Hook

Ask where the character stands on one setting institution that may matter later: the Knights of Solamnia, arcane magic, the old gods, elves, the scars of the Cataclysm, or the idea that another great war could happen.

GM Note

Do not correct character beliefs just because the player has chosen an inaccurate in-world assumption. False beliefs are useful characterization as long as the player understands the distinction.

pages.name: Ispin Greenshield: Make Him Personal
pages.html:
Every character knew Ispin personally. They need not have loved him in the same way, but nobody should be attending because "the adventure says so."

Choose or Invent the Relationship

MentorIspin taught you part of adventuring life.
RescuerIspin once got you out of serious trouble.
You Rescued HimYour version and his version differ dramatically.
EmployerIspin hired you for an early adventure.
Family FriendYou knew him before becoming an adventurer.
RivalCompetition became affection.
Traveling CompanionCircumstances kept you together long enough to matter.
StudentIspin decided he had something to teach you.
DebtorOne of you owed the other something never quite settled.

Ispin Questions

  1. What did Ispin call you that nobody else does?
  2. What did Ispin teach you?
  3. What did you teach Ispin?
  4. What story did he always exaggerate?
  5. What did he know about you that most of the party does not?
  6. What is the last thing you remember him saying to you?

The Keepsake

Each PC invents one mundane item from Ispin: a bent coin, bad compass, fishing lure, cracked mug, green ribbon, ridiculous IOU, piece of shield, badly drawn map, or anything equally personal. It has no mechanical value.

pages.name: Build the Party: Relationship Web
pages.html:
The party arrives at Vogler as a group with history, not as six strangers forced into the same scene.

Required Links

Every character creates one strong relationship and one complicated relationship with other PCs.

Strong Relationships

Friendship, loyalty, shared homeland, former colleagues, sibling-like bond, saved one another, traveled together, or mutual trust.

Complicated Relationships

Friendly rivalry, debt, ideological disagreement, old embarrassment, former romantic tension, failed business, secret resentment, or something one PC knows about the other.

For Each Link Answer

  1. What happened between you?
  2. Why do you still travel together?
  3. What does Ispin know about this that everyone else does not?

Boundary

Complicated does not mean hostile. A relationship that requires one PC to constantly sabotage another is not useful for this campaign.

pages.name: The Ispin Chronicles: Shared-History Workshop
pages.html:
Tell the players: "You have adventured together before. Tonight we are going to discover what actually happened."

Target

Create three stories if time allows. Two is the minimum. These are level-1 scale adventures: dangerous because the characters were inexperienced, not because they were fighting ancient dragons.

Record Each Story

Adventure NameGive it a memorable title.
What Really HappenedThe group's agreed version.
Ispin's VersionThe increasingly heroic retelling.
Who Saved WhomAt least one PC relationship.
Inside JokeSomething reusable at the funeral.
What We KeptA mundane souvenir.
NPC We MetSomeone who can become a later callback.
Unfinished BusinessOne loose end the GM may use later.

Foundry Record

Create or update a player-readable Journal named Our Adventures with Ispin. The important point is that Session 1 can draw directly from things the players invented tonight.

pages.name: Shared Adventure I: How We Became a Party
pages.html:
Ispin brought some or all of the characters together for a modest job. This is the first time the group discovered that they were better together than separately.

d12Adventure Seed
1A merchant wagon vanished on a supposedly safe road.
2Goblins occupied an abandoned tollhouse and demanded increasingly bizarre tolls.
3A child disappeared near a pre-Cataclysm ruin.
4Someone was impersonating a Knight of Solamnia.
5A flooded shrine contained something a local priest desperately needed.
6An ogre announced that a bridge belonged to him.
7A kender acquired an important map and then lost it again.
8An isolated farming family was terrorized every night.
9An abandoned watchtower showed lights after midnight.
10A merchant hired Ispin to escort cargo he very clearly lied about.
11A wounded magical creature was being hunted.
12Grave robbers disturbed something that should have remained buried.

Questions

  1. Who hired Ispin?
  2. Why did he bring these particular characters?
  3. What was the problem really?
  4. Who solved something nobody expected them to solve?
  5. Who made everything worse?
  6. What did Ispin later claim happened that absolutely did not?

pages.name: Shared Adventure II: Ispin's Terrible Idea
pages.html:
Begin with the sentence: "Ispin had a plan." Everyone should immediately understand why that sentence is worrying.

Build the Story

  1. The Objective: something sensible.
  2. Ispin's Plan: something much less sensible.
  3. The Point of Failure: when everybody realized the plan had collapsed.
  4. The Rescue: which PC got Ispin out?
  5. The Defense: which PC still argues that the plan technically worked?
  6. The Souvenir: what ridiculous physical reminder did the group keep?

Optional Complication Prompts

  • The disguise was immediately recognized.
  • The rope was twenty feet too short.
  • Ispin had misunderstood what "abandoned" meant.
  • The animal he intended to distract was much larger than described.
  • A local official arrived at exactly the wrong moment.
  • The item they were stealing was not the item they were hired to recover.

Payoff

This should become an inside joke the players can reference naturally during the road scene and funeral.

pages.name: Shared Adventure III: The Story Ispin Never Told Correctly
pages.html:
This is the story Ispin told so many times that his version became better known than the truth.

Version One: What Actually Happened

The party was frightened, confused, resourceful, and at least somewhat lucky.

Version Two: Ispin's Version

Every element has grown. Five goblins became fifty. A ditch became a canyon. A large wolf became a dire wolf, then an owlbear, and eventually perhaps a dragon. The mud became a battlefield. Someone's accidental shove became a heroic sacrifice.

Questions

  1. What detail grew the most with every retelling?
  2. Whose role did Ispin make absurdly heroic?
  3. Whose embarrassing mistake did he politely remove?
  4. What part did he always get exactly right?

A strong answer to the last question is something emotional and simple: "He always said we came back for each other."

pages.name: Character Finalization Checklist
pages.html:
Before switching into the playable prelude, freeze the administrative work. Everyone should be ready to simply play.

  • Name, pronouns, species, class, background.
  • Ability scores, proficiencies, equipment, languages, spells.
  • Token artwork and Foundry Actor ownership.
  • Short personal goal.
  • One strong PC relationship.
  • One complicated PC relationship.
  • Specific relationship to Ispin.
  • Ispin nickname and keepsake.
  • At least two shared Ispin adventures recorded.
  • Reason for coming to Vogler beyond "because the adventure starts there."

Final Question

Ask every player: "Why are you going to the funeral emotionally?" Grief, obligation, guilt, gratitude, curiosity, respect, unfinished business, or simply the realization that too much time had passed.

pages.name: Prelude Overview: The Last Road to Vogler
pages.html:
17 Darkember, 350 AC. The administrative Session 0 ends. The campaign begins quietly.

Purpose

Give the players 90–120 minutes to inhabit their characters before the main plot begins. There is no Dragonarmy attack, no Wayreth invitation awakening, and no Night of the Eye revelation tonight.

Scene Order

1. The Road15–20 minReunion and character descriptions.
2. One Last Little Problem10–15 minBroken cart; low-stakes cooperative play.
3. River Gate10 minFirst impression of Vogler.
4. Brass Crab10–15 minRooms, Yalme, and the weight of Ispin's name.
5. Free Exploration30–45 minChoose two or three village locations.
6. Supper15–20 minOld stories and last memories.
7. Night5 minEnd on the eve of the funeral.

GM Principle

The village must feel ordinary and worth remembering. The attack will matter later because tonight contains fish pies, bad ale, festival bunting, tired fishermen, awkward jokes, and people who expect tomorrow to be normal.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 1: The Road
pages.html:
Cold late-afternoon air follows the road toward Vogler. Harvest is over. Bare fields lie beyond low walls. Ahead, village smoke marks ordinary hearths rather than war.

Opening

The characters meet on the road several miles north of Vogler. They may have arranged the meeting in advance or simply catch one another on the final approach.

Spotlight Questions

  1. What do the others see as your character approaches?
  2. What has changed about you since the group last adventured together?
  3. What piece of Ispin are you carrying to the funeral?

Let Them Talk

Do not immediately introduce a problem. Give the group several minutes to recognize old friends, mention one of the freshly created adventures, and establish the rhythm of the party.

If Conversation Stalls

A wagon passes in the opposite direction. The driver recognizes Vogler's direction and asks whether they are going for "Greenshield's send-off." He has heard one absurd Ispin story and gets at least one detail completely wrong.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 2: One Last Little Problem
pages.html:
A farmer's cart has slipped partially into a roadside ditch. One wheel is damaged and two exhausted locals are trying to keep a frightened draft animal from making the situation worse.

No Initiative Required

This is a cooperative problem, not a combat encounter. Let characters use Strength, Athletics, Animal Handling, Mending, tools, rope, leverage, magic, or any reasonable plan.

Foundry Reinforcement

Use the scene to make each player perform one real check from their sheet. This quietly reinforces the technical training without announcing a tutorial.

Consequences

Failure does not injure anyone. It costs time, muddies clothing, breaks another piece of the cart, or forces a different approach.

Ispin Connection

When the travelers say they are going to Ispin's funeral, one farmer pauses: "Greenshield? Gods. That old liar still owed me a drink." After a beat: "Suppose he doesn't anymore."

pages.name: Prelude Scene 3: Arrival at the River Gate
pages.html:
Vogler should arrive as a place full of life. Festival preparations and funeral preparations coexist awkwardly because villages do not stop being villages when somebody dies.

First Impressions

  • Fishing nets drying.
  • Children weaving between adults carrying decorations.
  • Market stalls closing for the evening.
  • Hammering from the Village Circle.
  • A musician practicing the same short phrase badly.
  • The river and unfinished bridge beyond the buildings.
  • Kingfisher Festival decorations going up while tomorrow's funeral is also being prepared.

Ask the Party

"Before you go to the inn, what catches your character's attention first?" Let this answer determine which locations they are most likely to explore later.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 4: The Brass Crab
pages.html:
The Brass Crab is home for the night. Make it warm, slightly ridiculous, and immediately comfortable.

Yalme

Yalme has been given the party's names and knows Becklin expects them. She does not know them personally, but she knows they were Ispin's adventuring companions.

Rooms

Their rooms are already paid for. Dinner is not. Ispin apparently believed in hospitality with limits.

Breaking the Solemnity

After a sincere moment of recognition, Yalme should puncture it with something practical: "Right. No crying in the good mugs. They stain."

Information Available

  • The funeral is tomorrow morning.
  • Becklin is at Thornwall Keep handling arrangements.
  • The village is also preparing for the Kingfisher Festival.
  • The market is still partly open.
  • The Fishbowl will remain busy into the evening.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 5: Explore Vogler
pages.html:
Give the party roughly 30–45 minutes and let them choose two or three locations. Do not force a complete gazetteer tour.

The Market

Fish, produce, travel supplies, closing stalls, and festival decorations. Let PCs make mundane purchases and meet ordinary villagers. A kender craftsperson can offer something absurd and inexpensive that later survives as a souvenir.

The Fishbowl

Fishermen, fish pies, poor ale, and older locals. Someone knows one of the stories created during the shared-history workshop—but only Ispin's wildly exaggerated version.

Thornwall Keep

Briefly introduce Becklin Uth Viharin and Darrett Highwater. Becklin is busy with funeral preparations. She recognizes the party from Ispin's stories and references a detail invented earlier in Session 0. Do not run the full inheritance/green-shield material yet.

The Wharf

Boats return, nets are repaired, and a simple ceremonial boat is being made ready. Let the players notice it without explaining everything.

High Hill

A quiet old battlefield above the village. Use it for reflective conversation, not lore dumping.

Village Circle

Bunting, carpenters, food stalls, rehearsals, and normal friction. Introduce a few faces who can matter once the village is threatened.

Optional Micro-Encounter

A runaway dog steals an important-looking funeral ribbon, a child drops a festival lantern into the river, or two villagers argue over where Ispin's name belongs on a memorial board. Resolve socially or with one check; no combat.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 6: Supper and Stories
pages.html:
Bring the party back to the Brass Crab. Food and drink arrive. Give them space to talk without immediately steering the scene.

Prompts Only If Needed

  1. Which of Ispin's stories do you hope nobody tells tomorrow?
  2. When did you last actually see him?
  3. What would you have told him if you had known it was the last time?

Yalme's Story

Late in the meal, Yalme remembers Ispin spending an hour helping a child recover a toy boat trapped beneath the wharf. By evening he was telling people he had "rescued a Solamnic vessel from a deadly river monster."

The Point

Ispin's exaggerations wrapped themselves around acts of kindness. The party should leave supper understanding why ordinary people remember him fondly even when they roll their eyes at the stories.

pages.name: Prelude Scene 7: Night Before the Funeral
pages.html:
End quietly. Do not tease the Dragonarmy yet. The power of the ending is that nobody knows what is about to happen.

Closing Description

Festival preparations fade. Hammering stops one workshop at a time. The river continues beyond the dark windows. Somewhere downstairs, mugs are stacked and chairs dragged across the floor.

Final Question

Ask each player: "Before your character sleeps, what do they place beside the bed?" A weapon, spellbook, holy symbol, traveling boots, Ispin's keepsake, or something unexpected.

17 Darkember, 350 AC — Vogler.
Tomorrow morning, you bury Ispin Greenshield.

End Session 0

Do not roll directly into the funeral unless the group has explicitly scheduled an unusually long session. Let the line breathe.

pages.name: Session 1 Handoff and GM Checklist
pages.html:
Before the funeral session, harvest everything Session 0 created.

Record

  • Every PC's Ispin relationship.
  • Ispin nickname and keepsake.
  • Strong and complicated PC relationships.
  • Two or three shared adventures.
  • Each adventure's inside joke and unfinished business.
  • Vogler NPCs the players voluntarily engaged with.
  • Any purchase, promise, or small act of kindness made in the village.

Use at the Funeral

When the funeral invites stories, allow players to tell the adventures they created. NPCs can recognize Ispin's exaggerated versions. Becklin can know a detail that proves Ispin spoke about the party when they were absent.

Do Not Overwrite Their History

If a player invents a detail that does not break established campaign facts, accept it. The purpose of the exercise is shared ownership.

Technical Check Before Session 1

  • All Actors saved and backed up.
  • Tokens configured.
  • Blind death saves confirmed.
  • Potion macros or item usage aligned with house rules.
  • Critical rules understood.
  • Discord/Meet links in Useful Links.
